newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Austerity not antics pushed Ecuador Bucaram out.
newsitem.headline: Austerity not antics pushed Ecuador Bucaram out.

text.p: Ecuadoreans put up with Abdala Bucaram's eccentricities and antics but rebelled against a president who got elected on a populist ticket and tried to push harsh austerity down a poor country's throat.
Ecuador's Congress voted to oust Bucaram on grounds of mental incompetence on the second day of a 48-hour general strike against his economic belt-tightening measures.
Bucaram rejected his dismissal alleging it was unconstitutional and reminded the military he was still their top commander.

Despite being accused of being, among other things, a drunkard and a drug trafficker by his opponents, Bucaram came to power in this quiet Andean nation on a populist campaign that culminated in a July 7, 1996, victory based on massive support from the poor and Ecuador's native Indians.
Nicknamed "El Loco" -- "madman" in Spanish -- he released a rock-and-roll record soon after taking office.

His ample abdomen clad in a flashy black shirt and flanked by young female backup singers in tight-fitting midriff outfits, he belted out his 13 original tunes live in concert in the port city of Guayaquil.
Untroubled by any desire for a statesmanlike image, the 44-year-old Bucaram boasted he had always used rock'n'roll to seduce women, including his wife, with whom he has four children.
Bucaram also hailed Lorena Bobbit, famed for slashing off her husband's penis, as a defender of women's rights. "You are a person who knows how to defend her principles and values," he told her.

Trained as a lawyer, with a postgraduate degree in physical education, Bucaram began his political career in the Guayaquil town hall, where his duties included maintaining the port city's morals. Naturally he went about it in his own distinctive way.
Locals tell how Bucaram zipped around town on a motorcycle, intercepting young women and personally unstitching the hems of their miniskirts to make them longer.
"I do whatever the hell I like," he repeated while electioneering.
Postponing major economic announcements until later in the year, Bucaram gleefully pumped up the populist volume.
"I deserve to be called a Madman, in so much as I am a passionate man who loves his people blindly, but I am a man with a lot of common sense," Bucaram said once.

His unusual behaviour did not seem to hurt his standing until he began an austerity drive late last year. A private poll showed that 53 percent of Ecuadoreans thought he did a good job in his first 60 days in office.

But shortly after his inauguration, Bucaram sought the help of Argentina's former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, famous for taming his country's runaway inflation, to design an economic plan based on fiscal discipline and austerity.
The appointment by Bucaram of some friends and family members to key posts irritated his opponents.
But harsh austerity, including increases in electricity, telephone and public transport rates, late last year sparked social unrest in January.
The once superhero of the poor faced growing resistance from unions, especially oil workers who started legal actions against his energy minister, alleging corruption.
As soon as the 48-hour general strike began, unions announced they had decided to indefinitely extend the strike until they succeeded in pushing Bucaram out of his job.
